extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and practitioners interested in methods of scientific induction and experimental inquiry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative standards for using the principal methods of experimental induction (Method of Agreement, Method of Difference, Method of Concomitant Variations, Method of Residues) together with deduction and corroborating practices to infer causal laws in the physical and biological sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Infer causation when quantitative variations of an antecedent and a consequent run together; establish proportional or concomitant relationships between changing magnitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when antecedent and consequent vary together (e.g., capacity of neighboring body vs. charge in Leyden jar; qualities promoting dew). Caveat: when observed variations are restricted to narrow ranges, very different mathematical laws may produce similar numerical results within those limits, so extrapolation beyond observed limits is hazardous. Use broad ranges of variation and corroboration by other methods when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty in extrapolating laws beyond observed limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of variation observed within our limits of observation may not hold beyond those limits because new agents or properties might appear or because different laws may produce similar numerical results within narrow ranges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about extending an empirically deduced formula outside the domain of observation. Historical examples: empirically deduced formulæ for elasticity of steam and resistance of fluids failed when relied upon beyond the data range. When absolute amounts of variation are small relative to totals, numerical laws can be easily mistaken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where many varied instances exhibit the same effect, identify antecedents common to all those instances to infer a possible cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply by comparing diverse cases that share the effect but differ otherwise (e.g., Liebig’s cases of metallic poisons all show the metal combining with tissues into a compound resistant to putrefaction). Agreement establishes invariable co-existence but does not on its own determine direction of causation or exclusivity of the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare instances that are alike in all respects except one, where the presence of that single circumstance coincides with the presence (or absence) of the effect, to infer causal connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigorously requires a positive and a negative instance differing in only the single circumstance claimed to be causal. In practice this ideal is hard to meet; when met, it yields the strongest form of induction (direct proof of causation). Examples: antidotes that prevent a poison's effect when they remove the hypothesized antecedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect Method of Difference (Joint Method of Agreement and Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: When strict Method of Difference conditions cannot be satisfied, combine many agreement and difference instances to approach the certainty of the Method of Difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple instances and contrasts (e.g., many different antidotes that all share the incapacity to combine with tissues) to show that the proposed antecedent consistently correlates with the effect across varied contexts. This joint method can approach the certainty of strict difference but never fully replace a perfect single-variable contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of antidotes and comparative reagents as difference-cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ substances or treatments that prevent the putative antecedent from occurring (or neutralize it) to test whether the effect is thereby absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hydrated peroxide of iron neutralizing arsenious acid; sugar reducing copper salts; diluted sulphuric acid preventing lead-organic compounds. Such cases serve as difference-instances, but check that the antidote’s only relevant action is the prevention of the hypothesised antecedent (avoid hidden alternative mechanisms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of precise phenomenon-definition (preliminary operation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Precisely define and delimit the phenomenon under investigation before attempting induction (separate it from similar phenomena).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from dew: separate 'dew' from rain and fog by defining it as 'spontaneous appearance of moisture on substances exposed in the open air when no rain or visible wet is falling.' Proper definition ensures that comparisons and contrasts are meaningful and that methods are applied to the correct subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scales of intensity and systematic variation of single factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Expose materials or conditions in a systematic series to reveal gradients (scales of intensity) that indicate how a property correlates with the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: expose polished surfaces of various substances to reveal that those that conduct heat poorly are more strongly dewed; vary surface texture to reveal influence of radiative properties. This use of graded comparisons is a practical application of Concomitant Variations and helps isolate relevant causal qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration by Deduction from known laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Support and complete inductive inferences by deducing the observed effect from established physical laws when the relevant agents are known to be present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: deducing dew formation from laws of vapor pressure and heat transfer explains causation and exceptions (dry air) and thus strengthens inductive conclusions. Deduction supplies causative mechanism and can reveal additional necessary conditions missed by purely empirical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration by Controlled Experiment (experimental Method of Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Directly test causal hypotheses by experimentally introducing or removing the antecedent while keeping other conditions the same to see whether the effect appears or disappears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: cooling a surface in controlled conditions to find the temperature at which dew forms. Controlled experiments provide direct evidence of causation on a small scale and can be extrapolated with caution to larger scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration by Natural (or 'Nature-made') Experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit naturally occurring events that introduce a single, definable change in antecedents to observe resulting changes in effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: withdrawal of clouds briefly produces surface cooling and immediate dew deposition, functioning as a natural Method of Difference. Natural experiments can meet the strict requisites of difference when the natural change is single and rapid relative to other changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of multiple properties per substance when comparing different substances
rubrics_metrics.description: When difference-cases use different substances, each substance may have many properties; therefore a single nominal difference (substance A vs B) may obscure many real differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antidote examples: the peroxide might counteract poison via some other property than insolubility. To reduce this uncertainty, seek multiple independent antidotes or additional evidence that all such substances share only the property hypothesised to be causal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine multiple methods and lines of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations, Residues, deduction, controlled experiments, and natural experiments together rather than relying on any single method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations in the text show how the combined application (e.g., in the theory of dew and induced electricity) yields much higher assurance than any single method alone. Cross-method corroboration addresses limitations intrinsic to each method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues (and its relation to deduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for part of the phenomenon by known causes and assign the remaining 'residue' to unknown causes; this method is not independent of deduction but can be included among experimental methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that Residues relies on deductive subtraction (removing effects already explained by known causes) and so often requires prior theoretical knowledge; include it as part of the toolkit for direct induction when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct instances where positive and negative cases differ only by one circumstance
rubrics_metrics.description: The most conclusive induction arises from cases where positive and negative instances differ in the presence or absence of a single antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive in experimental design and case selection to match conditions as closely as possible, varying only the putative causal factor. When ideal single-difference cases are unattainable, be explicit about the resulting inferential limitations and use joint/indirect methods to compensate.
